name: Athenian Democracy
summary: Athenian democracy was direct rule by the adult male citizens, who met in the Assembly, filled most offices by lot and judged cases in large popular courts. It prized equality among citizens, free debate and public service, while excluding women, slaves and resident foreigners and holding an empire of subject states for much of the fifth century BC.
scope: Classical Athens from the reforms of Cleisthenes and Ephialtes through Pericles to the restored democracy of the fourth century BC, based on Pericles' Funeral Oration in Thucydides, Aristotle's Athenian Constitution and modern reference works. Excludes modern democratic theory and later revivals.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Athens policed the grain trade through magistrates and anti-hoarding rules because the city depended on imported grain; this is from general knowledge of the period and is not confirmed in the cited pages.

party-controls-media.rationale: Athens had no ruling party or press, and the Funeral Oration praises open debate and freedom in public life, so adherents would reject government control of information; inferred from that ethos.

party-commands-army.rationale: Athens had no parties; the citizen militia and fleet were led by generals elected by and answerable to the Assembly, so command by a party rather than the citizen body would be foreign; inferred.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Citizenship was tightly guarded (descent from Athenian parents, grants of citizenship rare and voted by the Assembly), so a long wait fits the spirit, though Athens had no residence path at all; inferred.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay for office and jury service let poorer citizens serve, and officials were ordinary citizens chosen by lot, though pay was a day wage rather than a stated cap.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Athens had no parties and prized free debate in the Assembly, so binding members would cut against its practice.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Inferred: Athens ran an empire of subject states under its own control and prized citizen self-rule, not sharing decisions in a binding union.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The sovereign Assembly decided war and policy, and the generals who commanded forces were elected and held to account by it; there was no head of state.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Athenian religion was civic, run by magistrates and citizen priesthoods, with no bishops or church hierarchy.

clerical-rule.rationale: Political authority rested with the citizen Assembly and courts; priests had no governing role.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Pericles' Funeral Oration calls on citizens to put the city first and die for it, and the citizens themselves were the government.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Inferred from Pericles' praise of free discussion and open comic theatre, though Athens did prosecute impiety, as in Plato's criticism.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Most offices were held once by lot, but generals such as Pericles were re-elected repeatedly; adherents would be split.

recall-officials.rationale: Officials were scrutinized before and after office, could be deposed or impeached by the Assembly, and ostracism removed leaders by vote.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Inferred: Athens led an alliance and empire that kept its forces abroad, so adherents would not withdraw from alliances.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Inferred: not addressed; resident foreigners rented homes and citizens held land, and nothing suggests Athenians wanted to ban renting.

people-in-arms.rationale: Athenian citizens served as soldiers and rowers themselves; Pericles boasts that Athens relies on its own citizens rather than on drilled foreign methods.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Not addressed; Pericles praises the city and many Athenians lived in the countryside, so adherents are split.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Not addressed; adherents of the polis had no doctrine on reunifying divided peoples.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Inferred: Pericles says Athenians cultivate the mind without losing practical action and that ordinary citizens judge policy well, so the educated are not set apart.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Inferred: Pericles calls Athens the school of Hellas, and Greeks regarded their culture as above that of outsiders.

death-penalty.rationale: Inferred: Athenian popular courts imposed the death penalty for grave crimes, and nothing in the democracy opposes it.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Anachronistic; Athenian women were excluded from public life and there was no school curriculum of this kind.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Not addressed; civic religion was central but there were no school curricula or creation doctrine, so adherents have no clear view.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Inferred: Athenian art and comedy were largely free of state restriction on erotic content, though not the subject of political doctrine.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Athens limited citizenship to those with Athenian parents, as the citizenship rules recorded in Aristotle and reference works show.

minority-language-support.rationale: Inferred: public business was conducted in Greek by the citizen body, and no support for other languages is recorded.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Inferred: the democracy enforced civic religion through impiety prosecutions and applied the same laws to all citizens.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Pericles says Athens does not frown on a neighbour for living as he pleases, so private diversity is welcomed, though adherents would not make it a goal.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Athens' Solonian tradition of shaking off debts suggests sympathy for relief, but it was domestic, so foreign-debt cancellation is inferred.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Anachronistic; Athenians defended polis independence but did not tie it to property transformation.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The sovereign Assembly and legislative boards (nomothetai) rewrote laws and constitutions, as in the 403 BC revision.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Athenian democrats prized free speech and equal participation, as in the Funeral Oration; inferred against suspending them.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Duties ran to citizens and the empire extracted tribute; global aid is inferred as foreign to the ethos.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Athens prized self-reliant defence of the polis; inferred, as nuclear weapons are anachronistic.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Democrats saw sortition, not elections, as the democratic method and elections as favouring the wealthy; there was no single head of state.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Public finance was controlled by the Assembly and councils; insulating money from popular rule is inferred as alien.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Not addressed; Athens' practice varied by circumstance.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Wealth was expected to serve the city through liturgies and Pericles praises public use of means, though private property was protected; inferred.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Anachronistic and not an Athenian question.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Ancient Athens had no concept of environmental risk, so it is left neutral as an inference.

collective-defense.rationale: Athens built its power on alliances such as the Delian League and defended allies, as the Funeral Oration's pride in aiding friends suggests; inferred.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Athens held an empire of subject states and settled its citizens on conquered land, so adherents would not call such control unlawful occupation.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Athenian religion was run by the polis, with magistrates overseeing sacrifices and festivals, so priests served the state; inferred.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Athens had no head of state, only annual officials chosen by lot or vote; the role is not applicable.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Athens suppressed revolts by allies such as Naxos and Thasos, and Pericles says the empire could not safely be let go.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Athens first let League members keep their own systems and later imposed its own; adherents are split.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Athens abolished kingship and held that power belonged to the citizens, so a divine ruler is alien to it.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Athens funded public needs through liturgies and levies on the wealthy rather than an equal rate; inferred.

character-from-environment.rationale: Athenian thought, including the Sophists, stressed both teaching and nature; no firm position.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Pericles says Athenians obey the laws, and Athens held its officials accountable under law, so no ruler was above it.

space-expansion.rationale: Not addressed in ancient Athens; inferred as indifferent.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Athenian democrats ruled through the Assembly, lot and popular courts, and rejected oligarchic or aristocratic elements.

leader-cult.rationale: Athens used ostracism to check over-mighty individuals and shunned tyranny, so mass cults of a leader were alien to it.

equal-parenting.rationale: Athenian law gave a father's household control of his children, so equal time for both parents is not supported; inferred.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Class conflict between rich and poor was a feature of Athenian politics, but socialism did not exist; inferred from the democracy's aim of citizen equality under law, not class war.

land-redistribution.rationale: Athens never made redistribution of estates part of its democracy; inferred from its respect for citizen property under law.

refugee-return.rationale: Athens restored exiles after civil strife; inferred that the democracy would accept return of those driven out.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Athens justified parts of its empire by kinship with Ionian cities, but citizenship was strictly civic and descent-based; adherents would be split on this anachronistic claim.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Athens prosecuted impiety, as in the trial of Socrates, so punishing religious dissent fits its practice; inferred since apostasy proper was not a legal category.

women-must-cover.rationale: Respectable women were secluded and veiled by custom, but this was social convention rather than something the democracy legislated; inferred.

common-currency.rationale: Athens pressed its allies to use Athenian coinage, so a shared currency suits an empire of one monetary standard; inferred.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The Greek poleis valued the independence of each city above any union of kin cities; inferred from the city-state model.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Athens had a single civic body and gave metics and foreigners no self-governing institutions of their own; inferred.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The question of minorities seeking rights or a homeland did not arise in Athens; left neutral as an inference.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Thucydides and Pericles present leadership, argument and civic values as shaping Athens, rather than economic change alone; inferred.

ban-cartels.rationale: Athens regulated grain traders to protect its supply, so state action against market manipulation fits its outlook; inferred.

no-bailouts.rationale: Athens relied on wealthy citizens for public burdens, but bailouts were not an issue it faced; left neutral.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Athenian popular bodies were sovereign and the Assembly and courts of ordinary citizens decided matters without a separate constraining judiciary, though later reforms added review of illegal proposals.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Women were excluded from citizenship and public office; inferred that equal representation would be unthinkable to a typical adherent.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Pericles boasts that the fruits of the whole earth flow into Athens, so the city's power rested on trade and empire rather than closing itself off.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Athenian citizens held no concern for binding international labor or environmental standards; inferred from its trading empire and slave economy.

moral-incentives.rationale: Pericles praises citizens who put public duty and honor above private gain; inferred that moral incentives suit this civic ethos.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Athens prized lawful, public decision-making and honored the overthrow of tyrants, not rule by armed conspirators; inferred.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Cleisthenes broke clan-based power and Pericles says office goes by merit and not by class, so inherited rank carried no political privilege.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Pericles' Funeral Oration praises the city's ancestors and its own way of life as the model for citizens, so history centred on Athens fits.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Pericles calls Athens the school of Hellas and defends its rule over allied states, so improving tutelage is inferred; the Athenians justified empire mostly by security and power.

patriotic-education.rationale: The Funeral Oration urges citizens to love the city and give themselves to it, so loyalty and pride are encouraged; formal schooling in them is inferred.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Not addressed; Athenian citizenship was by descent, but racial preferences are a modern issue with no ancient counterpart.

public-money-creation.rationale: Not addressed; Athens had coined silver but no banking system comparable to modern money creation.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Capitalism and its crises are anachronistic and not addressed.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Athens built and held an empire of subject states, and its tradition valued its influence over them, so cultivating influence in former dominions is inferred.

delink-world-market.rationale: Pericles says the fruits of the whole earth flow into Athens, and its trade and empire relied on integration with other states, so economic withdrawal is not in its spirit.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Marxist thesis not addressed; Athenians prized citizen equality and the empire paid for citizen pay, but no position is stated.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Pericles describes tolerance in private life and equality among citizens, but private discrimination was widespread, so adherents are split.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Assembly was sovereign and acted by majority, though a public suit could challenge an unlawful proposal, so an entrenched bill of rights is inferred to be disfavoured.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Classical Athens has no concept of colonial treaties of this kind; no inference is possible.

elective-rulers.rationale: Athenian offices were filled by lot or election from among citizens and the old hereditary kingship was gone; lot was preferred but generals were elected.

minority-veto.rationale: Decisions of the Assembly by majority vote bound all citizens, and ostracism could remove dissenters.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Athenians honoured tyrannicides and passed laws against subverting the democracy, and magistrates faced scrutiny; the statement is inferred from that.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The Assembly of citizens was sovereign in Athens and there was no monarch; the later primacy of laws over decrees complicates the picture.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Athenian sources do not address the matter; inference only.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Animals were routinely kept and used for food and sacrifice; humane limits are inferred.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Wealthy citizens paid for triremes and festivals through liturgies, and Pericles praises generosity to others.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Pericles says Athens regards the man who takes no part in public affairs as useless, not merely as quiet.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Athenians treated civic festivals and drama as education for citizens rather than a means of pacifying them; inferred.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: The democracy was understood as rule by the citizen body itself, so a ruling class that wins consent is not described; inferred.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Athens collected tribute from the allies of its empire and did not regard this as exploitation; inferred.

native-born-offices.rationale: Citizenship was limited to those of Athenian birth after 451 BC and only citizens held office; metics and foreigners were excluded.

party-own-road.rationale: Communist parties are outside the classical world; no inference possible.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Pericles boasts that the produce of the whole world flows into Athens through trade, so self-reliance was not the ideal.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Athens fought repeatedly for lost holdings such as Amphipolis; inferred from imperial aims.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Citizenship passed by descent from Athenian parents and resident settlers were kept out of politics; inferred.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Anachronistic; classical Athens had no fascism to be anti.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Anachronistic; the concept of totalitarianism does not apply.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Athens had no view on the American Civil War.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Athens honoured its heroes and also destroyed tyrants' memorials and houses; no clear rule.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Athenian public life excluded women and gave no thought to male disadvantage; inferred.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Women were under a male guardian in Athenian law and not equals in services or protection; inferred.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Pericles says Athens's constitution does not copy its neighbours' laws, while it serves as a model to others; adherents see institutions as shaped by the city's character.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Athenian strategoi were elected and held to account to the Assembly, and citizen-soldiers served under civilian rule.

paid-care-work.rationale: Household labour belonged to the oikos and to women and slaves and was unpaid; paying it is not envisioned.

missingStatements.text: Public offices should be filled by lottery among citizens rather than by election.
missingStatements.rationale: Most Athenian officials, and the Council of 500, were chosen by lot to secure equality and prevent vote-buying.

missingStatements.text: Citizens should be paid for serving on juries and in public bodies so that the poor can take part.
missingStatements.rationale: Pericles introduced jury pay and assembly pay followed, opening service to poorer citizens.
missingStatements.declined: Too narrow a mechanism of Athenian practice; its aim of enabling the poor to take part is already covered by priority-to-poor.

notes: Most economic and social statements were never addressed in antiquity and are low-confidence inferences, so the profile rests mainly on governance questions.
